rv.q: Terry Johnson's revival has energy and charm, with Tim Shortall's design evoking the period's extravagant fashions.
It’s a bawdy, colourful and amiably acted entertainment that can’t really take the weight of the art-v-life philosophising loaded onto it, but a jolly night out nevertheless.
The Libertine is an enjoyable, but rather unfulfilling play.
Not a full-on flop all told but be warned, if you go seeking after the elixir of lusty excitement you may end up feeling you've but quaffed a cup of Earl Grey.

Stephen Jeffrey’s play about famed hell-raiser, conversationalist and filthy poet John Wilmot (Dominic Cooper) is set during the reign of King Charles II and investigates Wilmot’s short-lived, adult life.
It is intermittently entertaining but the play never dips very deep beneath the surface.
The story of his life is shapeless and as a dramatic experience it ultimately feels a mite unsatisfying.

cn.t: Mixed reviews for The Libertine: Dominic Cooper's rakish swagger earns praise, but critics find the play itself underwhelming—more bore than libertine, failing to fully ignite the scandalous life of Rochester onstage.
